item.title: Ranking and Selection
item.dc:creator: Ziang Liu
item.description:
Define as a -dimensional system (decision variable), as the performance measure of interest, as the feasible region. Here, we consider the problem of finding the best system that minimizes the performance measure over the feasible region . The following optimization problem is often considered in simulation optimization:

Let be the best alternative among alternatives .

The objective of ranking and selection (R&S) is often to select the best system or a good system given the decision-maker’s tolerance Avci et al. (2023). Formally, we can define the precision measures as follows:

  • Probability of Correct Selection (PCS): The probability that the selected alternative is indeed the best one, i.e., .
  • Probability of Good Selection (PGS): The probability that the selected alternative is within a certain tolerance of the best one, i.e., .
  • Probably Approximately Correct (PAC): The probability that the selected alternative is within a certain tolerance of the best one, i.e., .

Rinott’s Two-Stage Procedure

The earliest indifference-zone procedure, due to Bechhofer (1954), assumes that all alternatives have a known, common variance. It takes a single stage of observations from every alternative, with chosen so that the alternative with the smallest sample mean is the best with probability at least whenever . When the variances are unknown, the required sample size depends on them, and no single-stage procedure can deliver the guarantee (Kim and Nelson 2006). Rinott (1978) therefore uses two stages. The first stage takes observations from every alternative and estimates its variance . The second stage brings the total number of observations of up to

so that alternatives with a larger variance receive more observations, and the alternative with the smallest overall sample mean is selected. The procedure is shown in Algorithm 1; the presentation follows Procedure 1 of Hong et al. (2021), adapted to minimization.

\begin{algorithm} \caption{Rinott's Two-Stage Procedure} \begin{algorithmic} \Require alternatives $\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_k$, indifference zone $\delta$, first-stage sample size $n_0 \geq 2$, confidence level $1-\alpha$ \Ensure $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_B$, the selected best alternative \State $h \leftarrow$ Rinott's constant for $k$ alternatives, first-stage sample size $n_0$, and confidence level $1 - \alpha$ \State Obtain $Y_j (\mathbf{x}_i)$ for $j = 1, \ldots, n_0$ and $i = 1, \ldots, k$ \State $S^2 (\mathbf{x}_i) \leftarrow \frac{1}{n_0 - 1} \sum_{j=1}^{n_0} \left( Y_j (\mathbf{x}_i) - \bar{Y} (\mathbf{x}_i;n_0) \right)^2$ for $i = 1, \ldots, k$ \State $N_i \leftarrow \max \left\{ n_0, \left\lceil \left( \frac{h S (\mathbf{x}_i)}{\delta} \right)^2 \right\rceil \right\}$ for $i = 1, \ldots, k$ \State Obtain $Y_j (\mathbf{x}_i)$ for $j = n_0 + 1, \ldots, N_i$ and compute $\bar{Y} (\mathbf{x}_i;N_i)$ for $i = 1, \ldots, k$ \Return $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_B$, the alternative with the smallest sample mean $\bar{Y} (\mathbf{x}_i;N_i)$ \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm}

The constant is known as Rinott’s constant. It is the solution of

where is the standard normal distribution function and is the density of the distribution with degrees of freedom. The equation has to be solved numerically; tables are given by Wilcox (1984). The constant increases with and decreases as or increases (Kim and Nelson 2006).

The guarantee rests on two observations. First, depends on the data only through , so by Stein’s theorem, conditional on , the sample mean is still normal with mean and variance , where follows a distribution with degrees of freedom. The second-stage sample size thus caps the standard deviation of every sample mean, up to the ratio , at . Second, the integral above is a lower bound on the probability that has the smallest sample mean in the least favorable configuration for all : the inner integral is the comparison of with one other alternative averaged over that alternative’s variable, the power treats the comparisons as independent, which is valid as a lower bound by Slepian’s inequality, and the outer integral averages over the variable of . Equating the bound to gives whenever . Since neither observation involves the true means, the same argument shows that the selected alternative is within of the best with probability at least under any configuration of the means, so Rinott’s procedure also delivers the PGS guarantee (Kim and Nelson 2006; Zhong and Hong 2022).

Every alternative receives its full second-stage sample no matter how clearly inferior it is, so the total sample size grows with both through the number of alternatives and through , and the procedure becomes expensive when is large. On the other hand, once the first stage is done, the alternatives never interact until the final comparison, so the second stage can be run on separate processors without any communication. This is why the KT procedure below uses it for the final comparison among the local winners.

The KN Procedure

Kim and Nelson (2001) proposed the fully sequential, indifference-zone selection procedure. After the name of the authors, this method is also known as Kim–Nelson (KN) procedure. The idea is to set a indifference zone , which is the minimum difference in performance that the decision-maker cares about. The procedure guarantees that the probability of correct selection is at least if the difference between the best and second-best alternatives is at least . Formally, this procedure guarantees that if , where is the second-best alternative.

Traditionally, the selection procedure is performed in a small number of stages, say 1, 2, or 3. The fully sequential procedure, on the other hand, collects one additional sample for each alternative in each iteration and screens them.

The procedure is shown in Algorithm 2. The presentation below follows Nelson and Pei (2021), in which the best alternative is the one with the smallest expected performance, . Kim and Nelson (2001) state the procedure for maximization, where the screening inequality is reversed.

\begin{algorithm} \caption{Fully Sequential, Indifference-Zone Selection Procedure} \begin{algorithmic} \Require alternatives $\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_k$, indifference zone $\delta$, first-stage sample size $n_0 \geq 2$, confidence level $1-\alpha$ \Ensure $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_B$, the selected best alternative \State $\eta \leftarrow \frac{1}{2} \left[ \left( \frac{2\alpha}{k-1} \right)^{-2/(n_0-1)} - 1 \right]$ \State $t^2 \leftarrow 2 \eta (n_0 - 1)$ \State $I \leftarrow \{\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_k\}$, $\quad r \leftarrow n_0$ \State Obtain $Y_j (\mathbf{x}_i)$ for $j = 1, \ldots, n_0$ and $i = 1, \ldots, k$ \State $S_{ih}^2 \leftarrow \frac{1}{n_0 - 1} \sum_{j=1}^{n_0} \left( Y_j (\mathbf{x}_i) - Y_j (\mathbf{x}_h) - \left[ \bar{Y} (\mathbf{x}_i;n_0) - \bar{Y} (\mathbf{x}_h;n_0) \right] \right)^2$ for all $i \neq h$ \Repeat \State $I_\text{old} \leftarrow I$ \State $W_{ih}(r) \leftarrow \max \left\{ 0, \frac{\delta}{2r} \left[ \frac{t^2 S_{ih}^2}{\delta^2} - r \right] \right\}$ for all $\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_h \in I_\text{old}$ with $i \neq h$ \State $I \leftarrow \left\{ \mathbf{x}_i \in I_\text{old} : \bar{Y} (\mathbf{x}_i;r) \leq \bar{Y} (\mathbf{x}_h;r) + W_{ih}(r) \ \ \forall \mathbf{x}_h \in I_\text{old} \setminus \{\mathbf{x}_i\} \right\}$ \If{$|I| > 1$} \State Obtain $Y_{r+1} (\mathbf{x}_i)$ and update $\bar{Y} (\mathbf{x}_i;r+1)$ for all $\mathbf{x}_i \in I$ \State $r \leftarrow r + 1$ \EndIf \Until{$|I| = 1$} \Return $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_B$, the single alternative in $I$ \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm}

Both and are computed once in the first stage and are never updated as more observations arrive; only the sample means and the counter change from one screening to the next.

As the algorithm proceeds, increases and decreases, reaching once . Once every pair has reached that point, that is, once , screening simply compares the sample means of the remaining alternatives, and all but the one with the smallest sample mean are eliminated. This bounds the run length: Kim and Nelson (2001) show that the procedure stops by , where .

MSS and MST Procedures

The KN procedure performs well in terms of the expected number of samples required to select the best alternative. However, Hong and Nelson (2005) indicated that the cost of switching among the simulations of the alternative systems should also be considered. They proposed two sequential indiindifference-zone selection procedures: the Minimum Switching Sequential (MSS), and the Multi-stage Sequential procedure with Tradeoff (MST).

KT Procedure

When the number of alternatives is large, the KN procedure becomes expensive in two ways. It takes an additional observation from every surviving alternative in each iteration, and it compares every pair of survivors after each observation, which requires comparisons on a single processor. Zhong and Hong (2022) proposed the knockout-tournament (KT) procedure, inspired by the bracket of a tennis tournament. The alternatives are paired up, each pair plays a match, the winner advances to the next round, and the loser is eliminated. About half of the alternatives are eliminated in each round, so the procedure stops after at most rounds. Each match is itself a run of the KN procedure on the two alternatives. Since the best alternative has to win every match it plays, the overall guarantee is obtained by allocating a probability of incorrect selection to each match in round , so that the allocations over all rounds sum to at most . The procedure is shown in Algorithm 3.

\begin{algorithm} \caption{Knockout-Tournament (KT) Procedure} \begin{algorithmic} \Require alternatives $\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_k$, indifference zone $\delta$, first-stage sample size $n_0 \geq 2$, confidence level $1-\alpha$ \Ensure $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_B$, the selected best alternative \State $I \leftarrow \{\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_k\}$, $\quad r \leftarrow 1$ \Repeat \State $\alpha_r \leftarrow \alpha / 2^r$ \State $I_\text{next} \leftarrow \emptyset$ \State Randomly pair up the alternatives in $I$; if $|I|$ is odd, add the unpaired alternative to $I_\text{next}$ \For{each pair $\{\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_h\}$} \State $\mathbf{x}_w \leftarrow$ \Call{KN}{$\{\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_h\}, \delta, n_0, \alpha_r$} \State $I_\text{next} \leftarrow I_\text{next} \cup \{\mathbf{x}_w\}$ \EndFor \State $I \leftarrow I_\text{next}$, $\quad r \leftarrow r + 1$ \Until{$|I| = 1$} \Return $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_B$, the single alternative in $I$ \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm}

Every match in Algorithm 3 is a fresh run of Algorithm 2 on the pair , with and replaced by . In particular, the first stage of KN, which takes observations from each alternative and computes the variance estimate , is repeated in every match. Observations that accumulated while winning an earlier round are not carried over. This is deliberate. The PCS guarantee of KN holds for an independent run, and reusing observations that helped an alternative win its previous match would bias the new match in its favor. Moreover, is the variance of the difference , which depends on the pair and has to be estimated anew for a new opponent anyway. Because only two alternatives are compared at a time, common random numbers can be used within a match simply by assigning the match its own random-number stream, and different matches can be run on different processors without any communication between them.

Discarding previous observations has a cost: for small , KN needs fewer observations in total than KT. However, there are matches in total, so each alternative plays fewer than two matches on average, and the number of observations a match needs does not depend on . Zhong and Hong (2022) show that the expected total sample size of KT is , which is the lowest possible growth rate for any procedure with a PCS guarantee, whereas that of KN grows faster than linearly in . In their experiments, KT requires fewer observations than KN once .

KT⁺ Procedure

In a parallel computing environment with processors, Algorithm 3 can be run by splitting the alternatives into subsets, letting each processor run the tournament on its own subset, and comparing the local winners at the end. Zhong and Hong (2022) propose two modifications for this setting, which give the KT procedure shown in Algorithm 4. First, a match may involve alternatives rather than two. When two clearly inferior alternatives with similar means are paired, KN needs many observations to separate them; with more alternatives in a match, it is unlikely that all of them are equally bad, and every clearly inferior alternative is eliminated quickly. The authors suggest fewer than alternatives per match when and about when . Second, a processor that has found its local winner would otherwise sit idle until the others finish. Instead, it uses that time to take enough observations from its winner, as prescribed by Rinott’s two-stage procedure (Algorithm 1), so that the final selection among the local winners can be made by comparing their sample means, without any further sequential sampling.

\begin{algorithm} \caption{Knockout-Tournament Procedure for Parallel Computing (KT$^+$)} \begin{algorithmic} \Require alternatives $\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_k$, indifference zone $\delta$, first-stage sample size $n_0 \geq 2$, confidence level $1-\alpha$, number of processors $m$, match size $g \geq 2$ \Ensure $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_B$, the selected best alternative \State Assign the alternatives to the processors in a round-robin fashion: $I^{(s)} \leftarrow \{\mathbf{x}_i : (i \bmod m) + 1 = s\}$ for $s = 1, \ldots, m$ \State $R \leftarrow \lceil \log_g (k/m) \rceil + 1$, $\quad \alpha_R \leftarrow \alpha / 2^R$ \State $h \leftarrow$ Rinott's constant for $m$ alternatives, first-stage sample size $n_0$, and confidence level $1 - \alpha_R$ \For{each processor $s = 1, \ldots, m$, \textbf{in parallel}} \State $r \leftarrow 1$ \Repeat \State $\alpha_r \leftarrow \alpha / 2^r$ \State $I^{(s)}_\text{next} \leftarrow \emptyset$ \State Randomly partition $I^{(s)}$ into groups of size $g$; the leftover alternatives, if any, form one smaller group, and a group of size $1$ advances directly to $I^{(s)}_\text{next}$ \For{each group $C$ with $|C| \geq 2$} \State $\mathbf{x}_w \leftarrow$ \Call{KN}{$C, \delta, n_0, \alpha_r$} \State $I^{(s)}_\text{next} \leftarrow I^{(s)}_\text{next} \cup \{\mathbf{x}_w\}$ \EndFor \State $I^{(s)} \leftarrow I^{(s)}_\text{next}$, $\quad r \leftarrow r + 1$ \Until{$|I^{(s)}| = 1$} \State $\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(s)} \leftarrow$ the single alternative in $I^{(s)}$ \State Obtain $Y_j (\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(s)})$ for $j = 1, \ldots, n_0$ \State $S^2 (\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(s)}) \leftarrow \frac{1}{n_0 - 1} \sum_{j=1}^{n_0} \left( Y_j (\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(s)}) - \bar{Y} (\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(s)};n_0) \right)^2$ \State $N_s \leftarrow \max \left\{ n_0, \left\lceil \left( \frac{h S (\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(s)})}{\delta} \right)^2 \right\rceil \right\}$ \State Obtain $Y_j (\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(s)})$ for $j = n_0 + 1, \ldots, N_s$ and compute $\bar{Y} (\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(s)};N_s)$ \EndFor \Return $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_B$, the local winner $\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(s)}$ with the smallest sample mean $\bar{Y} (\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(s)};N_s)$ \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm}

The per-processor part of Algorithm 4 is Algorithm 3 with pairs replaced by groups of size ; each group is again a fresh run of Algorithm 2 with and replaced by . The PICS per round is kept at rather than , since with the latter would leave most of unused. The final comparison is treated as one more round: is one more than the number of rounds a processor needs for its roughly alternatives, and the comparison receives the PICS , so the allocations over the tournament rounds and the final comparison again sum to at most . Rinott’s constant is the value for which, once every one of the local winners has observations, the one with the smallest sample mean is the best among them with probability at least whenever its mean is at least smaller than the others. It depends only on , , and , and is found by numerically solving an integral equation, so it is computed once before the processors start; Zhong and Hong (2022) write it inside the per-processor step, but it is the same constant for every processor. Note that the observations used in this final stage are, once more, taken afresh: the tournament observations of a local winner are not reused.

Zhong and Hong (2022) show that KT remains optimal in rate, that is, its expected total sample size is still for fixed and , although the constant grows with , because KN needs more observations in the worst case when a match contains more alternatives, and with , since in the extreme case the procedure reduces to Rinott’s procedure. In their experiments on Apache Hadoop, Apache Spark, and Google Cloud Platform with up to about alternatives, KT requires fewer observations and less wall-clock time than the good selection procedure (GSP) of Ni et al., the most efficient parallel procedure in the literature before it.

item.description:
Classification-based Policy Iteration

Lagoudakis and Parr (2003) proposed an classification-based policy iteration that uses classifiers such as SVM and neural networks to approximate the policy.

Lazaric et al. (2016) introduced cost-sensitive loss function weighting each classification mistake by its actual regret.

item.title: The Newsvendor Problem as a Multi Armed Bandit Problem
item.dc:creator: Ziang Liu
item.description:
The newsvendor problem is a classic inventory management problem in which a decision-maker must decide how many copies of a newspaper to order each morning. The demand for the newspaper follows a probability distribution. The overage cost occurs when the demand is less than the order quantity, and the underage cost occurs when the demand is greater than the order quantity.

Note that the classic newsvendor problem assumes that the demand distribution is known and by minimizing the expected cost, we can find the optimal order quantity.

Here, we assume that the demand distribution is unknown, and we can only observe the demand after ordering the newspaper. The objective is to minimize the cost over some time period. By considering the discrete order quantity as actions, we can model the newsvendor problem as a multi-armed bandit problem.

Symbol Description
Demand at time
Holding cost (overage cost)
Stockout cost (underage cost)

Experiments

In the following code, we solve an instance of the newsvendor problem using the simple bandit algorithm. In this example, , , and , where is discretized to the nearest integer.

We set the planning horizon steps = 2000. We use the -greedy policy with . We run the algorithm 10 times by setting number_of_runs = 10 and store the results in the rewards array. Finally, we plot the average reward over time.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


class newsvendor_as_bandits:
    def __init__(self, k, h, p, mu, sigma):
        self.k = k
        self.h = h
        self.p = p
        self.mu = mu
        self.sigma = sigma

    def bandit(self, action):
        # sample demand to integer
        demand = round(np.random.normal(self.mu, self.sigma))
        # calculate cost
        cost = self.h * max(action - demand, 0) + self.p * max(demand - action, 0)
        return -cost


class bandit_algorithm:
    def __init__(self, bandit, epsilon, steps):
        self.bandit = bandit
        self.epsilon = epsilon
        self.steps = steps
        self.k = bandit.k
        self.Q = np.zeros(self.k)
        self.N = np.zeros(self.k)
        self.reward = np.zeros(self.steps)

    def learn(self):
        for t in range(self.steps):
            # epsilon greedy
            if np.random.rand() < self.epsilon:
                action = np.random.randint(self.k)
            else:
                # choose action with maximum Q, if multiple, choose randomly
                action = np.random.choice(np.where(self.Q == np.max(self.Q))[0])
            # get reward
            reward = self.bandit.bandit(action)
            # update Q
            self.N[action] += 1
            self.Q[action] += (reward - self.Q[action]) / self.N[action]
            # update reward
            self.reward[t] = reward


if __name__ == "__main__":

    # set random seed for reproducibility
    np.random.seed(0)

    # parameters
    k = 10
    h = 0.18
    p = 0.7
    mu = 5
    sigma = 1
    optimal = 6
    epsilon_list = [0.1]
    steps = 2000

    # mean reward
    number_of_runs = 10
    rewards = np.zeros((len(epsilon_list), number_of_runs, steps))

    # newsvendor problem
    newsvendor = newsvendor_as_bandits(k, h, p, mu, sigma)

    for i in range(len(epsilon_list)):
        for j in range(number_of_runs):
            # initialize bandit algorithm
            bandit = bandit_algorithm(newsvendor, epsilon_list[i], steps)
            # learn
            bandit.learn()
            # store results
            rewards[i, j, :] = bandit.reward
            # print optimal action and Q value
            print(
                "optimal action = {}, Q = {}".format(
                    np.argmax(bandit.Q), bandit.Q[np.argmax(bandit.Q)]
                )
            )

    # plot
    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
    for i in range(len(epsilon_list)):
        plt.plot(
            np.mean(rewards[i, :, :], axis=0),
            label="epsilon = {}".format(epsilon_list[i]),
        )
    plt.xlabel("Steps", fontsize=14)
    plt.ylabel("Average Reward", fontsize=14)
    plt.title("Average Reward vs Steps", fontsize=16)
    plt.tick_params(axis="both", which="major", labelsize=12)
    plt.legend(fontsize=12)
    plt.show()

The newsvendor problem is a classic model in operations research. Imagine a newsboy who has to decide how many newspapers to buy each morning before knowing the actual demand. If he buys too many, he incurs a holding cost for unsold newspapers; if he buys too few, he incurs a penalty cost for lost sales. The objective is to find the optimal order quantity that minimizes the expected total cost.

The Feature-Based Newsvendor Problem

In many real-world scenarios, the demand may depend on certain features. For example, the demand for a product may vary based on the day of the week, weather conditions, or promotional activities. In such cases, the data can be represented as pairs of features and demand observations , where is the feature vector associated with the -th observation.

Note that we assume that the features can be observed before the order quantity is decided, while the demand is unknown at the time of ordering.

item.title: Bandit-Based Algorithm for Hyperparameter Optimization
item.dc:creator: Ziang Liu
item.description:
Machine learning models often have hyperparameters that need to be tuned for optimal performance. When the number of hyperparameters is large, it can be difficult to find a good combination of hyperparameters manually. Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) is a method for automatically searching for hyperparameter combinations that improve model performance.

HPO can be classified into the following categories:

  • Bayesian optimization
  • Bandit-based optimization
  • Evolutionary optimization / Metaheuristics

OZAKI et al. (2020) give a comprehensive review of HPO methods (the paper is written in Japanese). They also provide a guideline for selecting HPO methods based on the characteristics of the problem.

Bandit-Based Optimization

Successive Halving

Successive Halving was originally proposed by Karnin et al. (2013). Later, Jamieson and Talwalkar (2016) proposed to use this method for HPO.

Successive Halving requires a budget and a number of configurations . In the context of HPO for machine learning models, a configuration refers to a specific combination of hyperparameters. The budget can be defined as the total number of iterations that can be used. The performance of a configuration is evaluated by the loss function. In this algorithm, denotes the loss of configuration after iterations.

\begin{algorithm} \caption{Successive Halving} \begin{algorithmic} \Require Budget $B$, number of configurations $n$ \State $S_0 \leftarrow \{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ \For{$k = 0, 1, \dots, \lceil \log_2 n \rceil - 1$} \State $r_k \leftarrow \lfloor \frac{B}{|S_k| \lceil \log_2 n \rceil} \rfloor$ \State $R_k \leftarrow \sum_{j=0}^{k} r_j$ \State Run each configuration in $S_k$ for $r_k$ additional iterations \State Get $l_{i, R_k}$ for each configuration $i \in S_k$ \State $S_{k+1} \leftarrow \left\{ i \in S_k : l_{i, R_k} \text{ is among the best } \lfloor |S_k| / 2 \rfloor \text{ losses} \right\}$ \EndFor \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm}

Hyperband

In the Successive Halving algorithm, it is required to specify and in advance. However, it is may be difficult to choose a good value for in practice. Hyperband (Li et al. 2016) can be considered as a extension of Successive Halving.

\begin{algorithm} \caption{Hyperband} \begin{algorithmic} \Require $R$, $\eta$ \State $s_{max} \leftarrow \lfloor \log_\eta R \rfloor$ \State $B \leftarrow (s_{max} + 1) R$ \For{$s = s_{\max}, s_{\max} - 1, \dots, 0$} \State $n \leftarrow \lfloor \frac{B}{R (s + 1)} \rfloor \eta^s$ \State $r \leftarrow R \eta^{-s}$ \For{$i = 0, 1, \dots, s$} \State $n_i \leftarrow \lfloor n \eta^{-i} \rfloor$ \State $r_i \leftarrow r \eta^i$ \State Run each configuration in $S_i$ for $r_i$ iterations \State Get $l_{i, r_i}$ for each configuration $i \in S_i$ \State $S_{i+1} \leftarrow \left\{ i \in S_i : l_{i, r_i} \text{ is among the best } \lfloor n_i / \eta \rfloor \text{ losses} \right\}$ \EndFor \EndFor \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm}

Note that the original paper writes this step as , rounding up only at the end; here we use , which floors the per-round budget first and matches the values in the paper’s Table 1 and its reference implementation.

The following example is adapted from Li et al. (2016). Let and , so that . The following table shows the values of and for each value of .

def hyperband(R, eta):
    """Return the (n_i, r_i) schedule for each bracket s."""
    s_max = 0
    while eta ** (s_max + 1) <= R:
        s_max += 1
    B = (s_max + 1) * R

    brackets = {}
    for s in range(s_max, -1, -1):
        n = B // R // (s + 1) * eta**s
        r = R // eta**s
        brackets[s] = [(n // eta**i, r * eta**i) for i in range(s + 1)]
    return brackets

for i in range(s_max + 1):

Hyperband Variants

Later works have proposed several variants of Hyperband. There are two main directions for improving Hyperband. One direction is to combine Hyperband with metaheuristics. The other direction is to combine Hyperband with Bayesian optimization.

Awad et al. (2021) proposed DEHB, a hyperparameter optimization method that combines differential evolution and Hyperband. Differential evolution (DE) is a classic evolutionary algorithm and Hyperband is a bandit-based method for hyperparameter optimization.

DEHB has been shown to outperform other hyperparameter optimization methods on a variety of benchmark problems. Eimer et al. (2023) discussed the hyperparameter optimization problem in the context of reinforcement learning (RL). They conducted a experimental study on the performance of various hyperparameter optimization methods, including random search, DEHB, and BGT. Their results show that DEHB has a good performance. Eggensperger et al. (2021) developed a collection of multi-fidelity benchmark problems for HPO, called HPOBench. Their results also show that DEHB has a good performance.

Another variant of Hyperband is BOHB (Falkner et al. 2018), which combines Hyperband with Bayesian optimization.
